title: Why HashMap capacity is a power of two
context: Why does HashMap use a capacity that is a power of two?

source.title: JavaGuide (Snailclimb): Java collections questions (2 of 2)
source.note: Question and topic from this JavaGuide article. The answer is an original English write-up; see content/sources/javaguide/NOTICE.md.

answer: With a power-of-two capacity, the bucket index is `hash & (n - 1)`, a fast bit mask, instead of a slower modulo. Doubling keeps the mask valid, and each entry either stays in its bucket or moves to bucket plus old capacity, so resizing is simple. A power of two also spreads bits well when the hash is mixed. If you pass a capacity such as 100, HashMap rounds it up to 128.

points.title: Mask instead of modulo
points.why: A bit mask is faster than the modulo operation for each lookup.

points.title: Simple resize
points.why: Each entry moves to the same index or the same index plus the old size.
